data.hypothesis: The only earlier T1 candidate used 2,048-element tiles and produced 2,048 partials at n=4,194,304; it was correct and averaged 8.62 µs, but its source diversity is only one program. This contrasting 8,192-element tile should produce 512 partials at the target size, reducing CTA and final-CTA work while retaining enough blocks to process the input. For larger inputs, a bounded 2,048-partial cap and an extra reduction stage above 1,024 partials avoid an oversized final CTA. The performance tradeoff is unmeasured.

memory_lessons.applicability: Provides a valid comparison point, not evidence that the larger tile will be faster.
memory_lessons.claim: The baseline was correct on all ten checks and averaged 46.67 µs; the earlier T1 tiled reduction was also correct and averaged 8.62 µs. That candidate used 2,048-element tiles, so an 8,192-element tile tests a distinct partial-count and CTA-work tradeoff; its result is not yet measured.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Compare correctness and repeated timings for this tile configuration against the baseline and earlier T1 candidate.

data.notes: Only src/candidate.cu is changed; sources_kept is empty because no integration source ideas were supplied. The candidate uses default-stream launches and bounded scratch (at most 2,048 first-stage partials and eight group sums). No correctness or timing result is claimed for this candidate; the controller should evaluate it.
transformations: Replace modulo/shared-memory tree reduction with warp-shuffle reduction and a single inter-warp barrier.
Use 256-thread CTAs to accumulate 32 coalesced values per thread over disjoint 8,192-element tiles.
Cap first-stage partials at 2,048; reduce directly to out for up to 1,024 partials, and use a bounded grouped stage above that threshold.
Handle n<=0 with the additive identity, n=1 with a device copy, and n<=8,192 with one reduction CTA.
